result:
There is a strange kind of magic in the way a blank page waits for you. It doesn’t judge what you’re about to say, and it doesn’t care if you have a grand thesis or if you’re just rambling about the texture of the air on a Tuesday afternoon. It just sits there, an invitation to pull something out of the messy filing cabinet of the human mind and pin it down into words.

Lately, I’ve been thinking a lot about friction. 

We live in a culture obsessed with removing friction. We want one-click ordering, instant streaming, fast-charging batteries, and answers to any trivia question within three seconds via a glowing rectangle in our pockets. Friction is seen as the enemy of progress. If something is hard, tedious, or slow, our immediate instinct is to optimize it, automate it, or bypass it entirely.

And yet, so much of what makes life feel *real* happens in the friction.

Think about learning an instrument. The friction of clumsy fingers pressing into steel strings until your fingertips callus. Think about baking bread, where you can’t rush the rise; you have to wait for the yeast to do its quiet, invisible work. Think about relationships, where true intimacy only arrives after you’ve bumped up against someone else’s quirks, boundaries, and worldview, and decided to stay in the room anyway.

When you smooth away all the friction, you often smooth away the meaning, too. 

If a song could be generated instantly by thought alone, would it carry the same weight as one written at 2:00 AM on a cheap upright piano after a heartbreak? Maybe. But the struggle—the wrestling match between what you want to express and your current ability to express it—is usually where the soul gets baked into the project.

It’s like hiking versus taking a helicopter to the top of a mountain. Sure, from the peak, the view is technically the same. But the person who walked up earned the thin air. Their legs ache, their water bottle is empty, and they know every switchback of the trail. The view isn't just a visual stimulus; it’s a narrative.

Maybe that's why we still write, even when AI can stitch together sentences in milliseconds. Writing is the friction. It’s the process of figuring out what you actually think by watching the words appear on the screen. Half the time, I don't know where a paragraph is going until I'm three words deep into it. The surprise is the point.

So here’s to a little bit of friction today. May your coffee take just a minute too long to brew, may your walk have a slight uphill grade, and may you find yourself wrestling with a thought worth thinking.
